import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Kotzig's Conjecture

*Reference:* A. Kotzig, cited in A. Rosa, *On certain valuations of the vertices of a graph*,
Theory of Graphs (Internat. Sympos., Rome, 1966), Gordon and Breach, 1967, pp. 349–355.

Kotzig conjectured that for every $n$, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into copies of
any $n$-edge tree via cyclic shifts of a single embedding. This is strictly stronger than
Ringel's conjecture; see `Paper/RingelConjecture.lean`. The large-$n$ case is proved by
Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov; see `Arxiv/2001.02665/RingelConjecture.lean`.
-/
namespace KotzigConjecture

open SimpleGraph

/--
For any tree $T$ with $n$ edges, the complete graph $K_{2n+1}$ decomposes into
$2n+1$ edge-disjoint copies of $T$ via cyclic shifts of a single embedding.

The $2n+1$ copies are $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_{2n}$ where $f_i(v) = f_0(v) + i$ for all vertices
$v$ — each copy is obtained by adding $i \pmod{2n+1}$ to every vertex of the base copy.
This is strictly stronger than `RingelConjecture.ringel_conjecture`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem kotzig_conjecture {V : Type} [Finite V]
    (T : SimpleGraph V) (hT : T.IsTree)
    (n : ℕ) (hn : T.edgeSet.ncard = n) :
    ∃ f : Fin (2 * n + 1) → (V ↪ Fin (2 * n + 1)),
      (∀ i v, f i v = f 0 v + i) ∧
      Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (T.map (f i)).edgeSet (T.map (f j)).edgeSet) ∧
      ⨆ i, T.map (f i) = (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (2 * n + 1))) := by
  sorry

end KotzigConjecture

reformulations.difference: The Lean statement uses an edge partition by cyclically translated embeddings, rather than the equivalent rainbow embedding in the near-distance colouring (or ρ-valuation) described by Montgomery–Pokrovskiy–Sudakov and Rosa's result as reported by Gallian.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Put m = 2n+1. The unordered edges of K_m split into n translation orbits, indexed by their cyclic distances 1,…,n. Each orbit has m edges: an unordered edge has no nonidentity translation stabilizer because m is odd. A rainbow embedded n-edge tree selects exactly one edge from each orbit, so its m translates partition all host edges. Conversely, two base edges of the same cyclic distance would be translates of one another and cause overlap between two distinct copies, contradicting the Lean pairwise-disjointness condition. Fin addition is precisely addition modulo m. Although T.map f uses the full host vertex type, its restriction to Set.range f is isomorphic to T, and vertices outside that image contribute no edges. Thus this encoding imposes exactly the intended cyclic decomposition.

sources_consulted: Montgomery, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov, A proof of Ringel's Conjecture, arXiv:2001.02665v2, §1: https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02665 and LaTeX source https://arxiv.org/e-print/2001.02665.
Gallian, A Dynamic Survey of Graph Labeling, 28th edition (October 30, 2025), §§1, 2.1, 3.3 and reference [2986]: https://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/viewFile/DS6/pdf.
Gnang, A proof of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa Conjecture, abstract and version history only: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03178.
review.notes: No mathematical defects found. In /workspace/review/scratch.lean and boundaries.lean, Lean checks confirmed finiteness of the edge set, exclusion of empty trees, the identity |V| = n+1, modular addition, the general n=0 case, and concrete decompositions for n=1 and n=2. Also proved the equivalence between a cyclic family and a single base embedding, the equivalence between disjoint coverage and unique edge coverage, and the isomorphism of each mapped graph restricted to its image with T. The full rainbow/ρ-valuation equivalence above was checked mathematically, not proved in Lean. Rosa's original 1967 scan could not be retrieved: the link supplied by Gallian returned an access restriction. Its relevant formulation is corroborated explicitly by MPS §1 and Gallian §3.3. No confirmed status defect: MPS proves the sufficiently-large-n case, not the all-n statement. Gallian mentions Gnang's stronger graceful-tree proof claim, but the consulted material does not establish its acceptance; Wikipedia still records that conjecture as open.
